entry.content:
O&M Newsletter, August 2026

Maine Department of Environmental Protection sent this bulletin at 08/05/2026 04:12 PM EDT

AUGUST 2026

In this issue:

  • Breaking: Active Cyber Breaches Affecting Public Water Systems Demand Immediate Action.
  • CISA Alert to Water and Wastewater Systems Regarding Cybersecurity Threats.
  • Stay Informed: Key Updates on Rulemaking for Chapters 595 and 579!
  • State Laboratory Certification Required for In-House Testing of Nitrogen and Phosphorus Samples.
  • EPA Announces WIFIA Application Fee Waiver for Small Communities.
  • DMR-QA 2026 Update.
  • Training Highlights.
  • For Practice.

Breaking: Active Cyber Breaches Affecting Public Water Systems Demand Immediate Action.

The US EPA, FBI, Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), and Water Information Sharing & Analysis Center (WaterISAC) have held urgent briefings regarding active and on-going cybersecurity breaches at dozens of Public Water Systems (PWSs) in at least seven states across the U.S. The targeted PWSs range in size from small to large.

Many wastewater systems use similar technology as found in the drinking water sector. A common symptom of these breaches includes a loss of PLC connectivity with devices. These incidents all involve vulnerabilities related to PLCs, as described in the Iranian-Affiliated Cyber Actors Exploit Programmable Logic Controllers Across US Critical Infrastructure advisory (PDF).

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has information and guidance regarding malicious cyber actors targeting PLCs.

entry.title: Maine DEP Issues Air Quality Alert as Particle Pollution Levels Predicted to Escalate to Unhealthy Ranges
entry.content:
Maine DEP Issues Air Quality Alert as Particle Pollution Levels Predicted to Escalate to Unhealthy Ranges

Maine Department of Environmental Protection sent this bulletin at 07/17/2026 03:23 PM EDT

--- PRESS RELEASE ---

For Immediate Release

 

Maine DEP Issues Air Quality Alert as Particle Pollution Levels Predicted to Escalate to Unhealthy Ranges

 

AUGUSTA, July 17, 2026 — The Maine Department of Environmental Protection warns that ground-level particle pollution concentrations are forecasted to reach the ‘Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups’ (USG) level this Saturday due to wildfire smoke drifting in from Manitoba and Ontario, Canada.

The smoke plume is expected to move back over Maine during the day on Saturday, with air quality measured by a 24-hour average forecasted at the USG level. Some hours may experience particle pollution levels even higher than this range. Residents are encouraged to follow health recommendations that suit their individual needs.

Smoke conditions may improve by midday Sunday, but due to the unpredictable nature of wildfire smoke, the Maine Department of Environmental Protection advises checking their website or calling the toll-free Air Quality Hotline at 800-223-1196 for the latest updates throughout the weekend.

Elevated particle pollution levels can affect sensitive groups such as children, older adults, outdoor workers, and individuals with respiratory or heart conditions including asthma, bronchitis, and COPD. Symptoms may include coughing, shortness of breath, throat irritation, and mild chest pain. Even healthy adults engaging in outdoor physical activity might notice these effects.

Some actions you can take to protect your health during such periods include:

  • Avoiding strenuous outdoor activity
  • Closing windows and circulating indoor air with a fan or air conditioner
  • Asthmatics should keep their quick-relief medications and action plan handy

Additional health information may be found on the following websites:

  • Maine CDC asthma prevention and control
  • USEPA's asthma control and management
  • AIRNOW for smoke impacted areas

entry.title: Expanding Local Food Production and Agriculture Education Across Maine
entry.content:
Hello, this is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

Well, you know, one of the lessons learned from the pandemic time was how dependent we are as a state and community on producers from other states and other countries for basic goods like food, textiles, and construction materials. It occurred to me that our growing season is too incredibly short for us to become as self-reliant as we should be.

And after the pandemic disrupted markets and caused food shortages nationwide, we realized it was very important to have locally grown, fresh food right here in Maine and help our local farmers. So I used federal funding through my Jobs and Recovery Plan to provide grants to farmers to buy equipment to meet that higher demand for locally grown food, and I began to look for other ways to extend our growing season here in Maine.

Well, one of the things you can do is to provide greenhouses to communities who are able to support them and help people of all ages learn how to grow their own food. I called on the Legislature to provide one-time funds through the state biennial budget to buy greenhouses for as many schools and communities as possible. That will strengthen our supply of local food and will teach kids and families to grow their own food and extend the growing season.

The Legislature funded that proposal, and I'm proud to announce that we're now awarding grants to communities across Maine to expand their local food production and education programs through durable shared-use greenhouses. These grants were awarded through a competitive process. The organizations applied for them, and they include the Alfond Youth and Community Center in Waterville, where they're going to install a greenhouse to expand local food production and youth education. 

The Healthy Island Project in Stonington will use a greenhouse to increase access to fresh, locally grown food. And the Portland Community Squash will install a greenhouse to send more fresh produce home to low-income families and teach Portland Public School students how to grow their own food. Limestone Community School will install a greenhouse to expand their outdoor science program and provide students with hands on learning in nutrition, agriculture, and environmental science. And they'll run a student-run farmers market—I think that's great.

Over the past eight years, my Administration has invested more than $60 million in Maine farms and local agriculture, supporting the purchase of locally grown food, helping farmers expand their operations and equipment, strengthening our food system, and keeping Maine's farming heritage thriving.

You know, my grandparents were potato farmers in Ashland. I hope they would be proud that their granddaughter insisted that the state budget include a small amount of money for community greenhouses across the state. Sort of like the Victory Gardens of World War II and decades past, places where people of all ages can learn something about nutrition and how to grow lettuce, peppers, and parsley; where the older folks can teach the younger folks about the value of homegrown tomatoes and cucumbers and such and talk with each other in community. Where they can feel the joy of growing their own healthy food and appreciate what their neighbors are doing and appreciate their own Maine roots, the way I appreciate mine.

Dave Mallett, one of my good friends, the singer who passed away last year, used to sing a very popular song: "Inch by inch, row by row. Gonna make this garden grow. All it takes is a rake and a hoe and a piece of fertile ground."

Well, we're going to have everybody singing those songs in Maine in honor of Dave Mallett, and in honor of our agricultural heritage and the state of Maine's ability to become independent and self-reliant by community greenhouses.

This is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

entry.title: USDA Distributes Oral Rabies Vaccine for Wildlife in Northern Maine
entry.content:
Aug 11, 2026

In cooperation with the Maine Department of Health and Human Services’ Center for Disease Control and Prevention (Maine CDC), officials from U.S. Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) Wildlife Services will distribute oral rabies vaccine (ORV) baits this week. USDA Wildlife Services will distribute nearly 599,000 ORV baits in Aroostook County from August 12 through August 24.

The fall ORV bait distribution follows this past spring’s distribution and is in response to continued rabid raccoon detections in Aroostook County. The USDA’s Wildlife Services spreads ORV baits to reduce the spread of the raccoon rabies virus in Maine. The baits help limit the potential for human and domestic animal exposures to the rabies virus through contact with infected wild animals.

Crews will spread the bait by air in rural areas and by vehicle in more populated areas. Each bait is a fishmeal-coated cube or sachet about one to two inches in size. Although humans and pets cannot get rabies from contact with the bait, they should not touch or move them.

Studies show that ORV baits are safe in many species of animals, including domestic dogs and cats. While dogs may get upset stomachs if they eat a lot of bait, there are no known long-term health risks. If a person has skin contact with a bait cube or sachet, rinse the affected area with warm water and soap. For concerns about a person or pet touching or eating a bait, call the Maine CDC’s 24-hour line at 800-821-5821.

Since 2003, the USDA’s Wildlife Services has worked to halt the spread of raccoon rabies in northern Maine. They also collaborate with Canadian officials in New Brunswick and Quebec to reduce the presence of rabies across Maine and Canada. The ORV bait distribution program in Maine is part of a larger effort by the USDA’s Wildlife Services to prevent the westward spread of raccoon rabies. This effort creates a barrier along the Appalachian Mountains from the Canadian border to Alabama.

Rabies is a virus that infects the nervous system of humans and other mammals. It spreads mainly through a bite from an infected animal. Once symptoms develop, rabies is almost always fatal. Timely post-exposure treatment can prevent disease in people. Approximately 90 percent of reported animal rabies cases in the U.S. occur in wildlife. As of August 10, 2026, 28 animals tested positive for rabies this year in 12 counties across Maine. These animals include raccoons, skunks, foxes, bats, and a goat.

To help protect yourself and your pet against rabies:

  • Keep your pets and livestock up to date on rabies vaccinations.
  • Feed pets indoors.
  • Keep garbage cans or other sources of food tightly secured.
  • Do not feed, touch, or adopt wild animals. Be cautious of stray dogs and cats.
  • Do not move wildlife. This can spread rabies into new areas.
  • Wash bite or scratch wounds with soap and water for 10 to 15 minutes.

Who to contact:

  • If an animal bites or scratches you, contact a health care provider.
  • If an animal bites or scratches your pet, contact your veterinarian.
  • To report a dead or suspicious-acting animal in northern Maine, contact the USDA’s Wildlife Services. In other parts of Maine, contact the nearest Maine Regional Communications Dispatch Center.

For more information:

  • USDA Rabies webpage
  • Maine CDC Rabies webpage
  • USDA Wildlife Services: 1-866-487-3297
  • Maine CDC disease reporting & consultation line: 1-800-821-5821 (available 24/7)

Photo of bait types: The bottom two bait types in the photo are a fishmeal-coated sachet(bottom) and cube(middle) and are the only two used in this ORV bait drop in Maine.

entry.title: Juanita C. Clark v. Town of Phippsburg
entry.content:
MAINE SUPREME JUDICIAL COURT Reporter of Decisions Decision: 2026 ME 85 Docket: Sag-25-553 Submitted On Briefs: June 16, 2026 Decided: August 13, 2026
Panel: MEAD, LAWRENCE, DOUGLAS, and TAUB, JJ., and HORTON, A.R.J.
JUANITA C. CLARK
v.
TOWN OF PHIPPSBURG
DOUGLAS, J. [¶1] Juanita C. Clark appeals from a judgment of the Superior Court (Sagadahoc County, Billings, J.) dismissing her complaint for review of the Town of Phippsburg Board of Selectmen ’s actions in connection with a neighboring property owner’s alleged violations of a cease-and-desist order and the Town’s land use ordinance. Natural Resources Disaster Relief Assistance Program (NRDRAP) applications Open today, Friday, August 14

August 14, 2026

The Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry (DACF) is opening applications for the Natural Resources Disaster Relief Assistance Program (NRDRAP) today, Friday, August 14, 2026.

Maine farmers, forestry businesses, aquaculture producers, and other eligible producers who experienced weather-related losses in 2023 or 2024 may qualify for financial assistance.

Eligible losses may include crop loss, aquaculture loss, standing timber loss, harvested timber loss, on-farm and forestry infrastructure loss, and bare-ground practices necessary to mitigate land loss.

Application period: August 14, 2026, through November 6, 2026.

Applications will be accepted through the online portal. Paper applications are available upon request.

Producers can prepare now. Applicants are encouraged to begin gathering documentation, including:

  • Ownership or lease documentation
  • Parcel ID information
  • FSA Farm Number, if applicable
  • Tax or business identification information
  • Photos or records documenting damage

Other records related to weather-related losses in 2023 and/or 2024 DACF will provide technical assistance throughout the application period. Virtual office hours will be held every Friday from 11:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. beginning August 14.

For updates, eligibility information, and application details, visit maine.gov/dacf/nrdrap, email NRDRA.DACF@maine.gov, or call (207) 530-3144.

entry.title: Friends of Eastern Bay v. Department of Marine Resources et al.
entry.content:
MAINE SUPREME JUDICIAL COURT Reporter of Decisions Decision: 2026 ME 90 Docket: BCD-25-337 Argued: March 3, 2026 Decided: August 18, 2026
Panel: STANFILL, C.J., and MEAD, CONNORS, DOUGLAS, and LIPEZ, JJ., and HJELM, A.R.J.
FRIENDS OF EASTERN BAY
v.
DEPARTMENT OF MARINE RESOURCES et al.
DOUGLAS, J. [¶1] In October 2024 , the Commissioner of the Maine Department of Marine Resources granted Acadia Aqua Farms ’ application for a twenty-year aquaculture lease of 19.71 acres in the coastal waters of Eastern Bay off Mount Desert Island for the cultivation of blue mussels and other shellfish. Friends of Eastern Bay, one of the intervenors in the proceeding before the Department, appeals from a judgment entered in the Business and Consumer Docket (McKeon, J. ) affirming the Commissioner’s decision granting Acadia’s application for the lease. We affirm the judgment. 2 I. BACKGROUND [¶2] In November 2019 , Acadia applied for a twenty -year standard aquaculture lease1 of 48.11 acres of coastal water in Eastern Bay, located in an area approximately 1,000 feet from shore southwest of Googins Ledge in the town of Bar Harbor. Acadia proposed to culture blue mussels using a floating pipe system at the water’s surface with nets hanging down in the water column to collect blue mussel seed. The mussel seed would be harvested using specially designed machiner y that is lowered over the collecti on netting to remove the seed with a brushing mechanism. The harvesting machine uses a hydraulic system to then pump the seed into a seventy -four-foot transport vessel. [¶3] Acadia intends to use the harvesting machine seasonally, from May to October, for up to a total of three weeks during those months. W hen not in use, the machine would be stored on a twenty-foot-by-twenty-foot floating raft permanently moored within the lease sit e. During the off -season, the harvesting machine may be removed from the lease site.

The Department of Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry (DACF) has opened a public comment period on a draft document that identifies conservation strategies for late-successional and old-growth (LSOG) forests in Maine. Maine's 132nd Legislature passed LD 1529, charging the DACF with developing a comprehensive report on statewide strategies to enhance the conservation of LSOG forests, including the management of transitioning late-successional forests. Public feedback is an important step in preparing the LSOG Conservation Strategies document for the Maine legislature, as it will further broaden feedback. entry.title: US Labor Department finds Wisconsin food manufacturer repeatedly exposed workers to safety hazards following 2 incidents, 3 fatalities
entry.content: JANESVILLE, WI – The U.S. Department of Labor has cited a Wisconsin-based food products manufacturer after two incidents involving industrial kettles releasing hot steam and liquid, causing three worker deaths and two serious injuries.Investigators with the department’s Occupational Safety and Health Administration responded to the first incident on Feb. 12, 2026, at IPMF LLC, operating as NaturPak. The incident involved the lid of an industrial kettle unexpectedly opening after a clogged vent line led to pressure building up, and then releasing steam, liquid, and organic material onto two employees nearby. One of the employees was also struck by an object and suffered a concussion. Both employees were hospitalized, and one later passed away because of complications from their injuries. A month later, OSHA investigators responded to another incident involving multiple worker hospitalizations on March 18, when a kettle lid opened while under pressure releasing steam, hot liquid, and organic material, burning three workers. Two workers were fatally injured and another hospitalized. OSHA issued the employer one serious citation for the design and usage of kettles leading to pressure and thermal burn hazards; a repeat citation for exposing workers to falls to lower levels; and an other-than-serious citation for failing to notify employees working adjacent to permit-required confined spaces.OSHA also issued serious citations for exposing workers to thermal hazards without quick access to emergency water. The employer also received citations for exposing workers to falls into the kettles and for failure to assess personal protective equipment for thermal risks. In addition, OSHA issued repeat citations for failure to develop, document, and utilize lockout/tagout procedures for the kettles and failure to train employees on lockout/tagout procedures. The agency issued citations with $115,850 in penalties related to the inspection opened on Feb. 12 and $248,250 in penalties for the inspection opened on March 18. IPMF LLC has 15 business days from receipt of its citations and penalties to comply, request an informal conference with OSHA’s area director, or contest the findings before the independent Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission. Please check the OSHA establishment search page periodically for any changes in the inspection or penalty status.

entry.title: Air Plan Approval; Maine; Chapter 140: Part 70 Air Emission License Regulation
entry.content: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is approving a Clean Air Act (CAA) operating permit program revision submitted by the State of Maine. This revision makes minor changes to Maine's operating permit program that are considered clarifications, that correct grammar, that codify longstanding practices, or that are necessary for the state to utilize an expected future electronic application system. entry.title: Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act Provisions; Fisheries of the Northeastern United States; Northeast Multispecies Fishery; Framework Adjustment 72
entry.content: NMFS issues this interim final rule to implement Framework Adjustment 72 (Framework 72) to the Northeast Multispecies Fishery Management Plan (FMP), specifically to implement status determination criteria for Georges Bank yellowtail flounder, set catch limits for multispecies (groundfish) stocks, and revise the process for setting recreational measures for Atlantic cod and haddock. This action is necessary to respond to updated scientific information and to achieve the goals and objectives of the FMP. The measures are intended to help prevent overfishing, rebuild overfished stocks, achieve optimum yield, and ensure that management measures are based on the best scientific information available.

The EPA is proposing to approve 35 IAC parts 217, 218, and 219 as satisfying the Moderate Volatile Organic Compound (VOC) RACT and NO<inf>X</inf> RACT requirements as well as Serious NO<inf>X</inf> RACT requirements for the Chicago, IL (Cook County, DuPage County, Grundy County, Kane County, Kendall County, Lake County, McHenry County, and Will County) and Metro-East St. Louis (Madison County, Monroe County, and St. Clair County) nonattainment areas under the 2015 ozone National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS or standard).

entry.title: Response to Clean Air Act Section 176A Petition From New Hampshire
entry.content: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing to grant a Clean Air Act (CAA or Act) petition submitted by the state of New Hampshire on December 24, 2025. The petition requests that the EPA remove the State of New Hampshire from the Ozone Transport Region (OTR) based on New Hampshire's continued attainment of the ozone National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) and technical analyses demonstrating that the additional control of emissions from the state will not significantly contribute to ozone attainment in any area in the OTR. The OTR was established by the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments and included the States of Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Vermont, the District of Columbia, and portions of northern Virginia.

Maine's Fall Foliage Season Set to Begin with Weekly Reports, New Event Feature

August 24, 2026

First 2026 foliage report arrives September 9; communities and organizations invited to share fall events with foliage visitors

Augusta, MAINE - One of Maine's most anticipated seasons is just around the corner, bringing brilliant color, harvest traditions, and countless reasons to explore the state.

The Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry (DACF) will launch its 2026 fall foliage reporting season on Wednesday, September 9, at MaineFoliage.com and by email to subscribers. Reports will be issued each Wednesday throughout the season, tracking the progression of fall color from northern Maine and higher elevations southward toward the coast.

This year, DACF is adding another way to help residents and visitors experience fall in Maine: organizations, communities, and event organizers are invited to submit fall events for consideration for inclusion in the weekly foliage reports.

"Fall foliage is more than something to see, it's an invitation to experience Maine," said DACF Commissioner Amanda Beal. "Whether that means visiting a farm, hiking a trail, attending a harvest festival, exploring a downtown, or simply following a scenic by-way, our weekly reports help people follow the color and discover more of Maine along the way."

2026 Fall Foliage Season Preview

DACF Maine Forest Service experts expect peak fall foliage to develop along its typical progression from north to south, with trees at higher elevations generally developing color before those at lower elevations.

Maine's tremendous diversity of tree species, landscapes, and growing conditions helps create both its spectacular fall color and an extended viewing season. Northern and coastal areas offer striking contrasts between evergreens and colorful maples, birches, and oaks, while inland forests provide a broad palette of fall color set among Maine's abundant lakes, rivers, mountains, and working landscapes.

While foliage conditions can vary from one location to another, Maine's healthy and diverse forests continue to provide outstanding opportunities for fall color.

"The great thing about fall foliage in Maine is that there isn't just one place or one moment to experience it," said MFS Director and State Forester Patty Cormier. "Color develops at different times across the state and across different landscapes. If conditions aren't at their best in one location, spectacular foliage is often just down the road."

Fall color develops through a combination of shorter daylight, cooler temperatures, leaf pigments, moisture, and other environmental conditions. As days shorten, trees slow their production of chlorophyll, revealing the yellow and orange pigments already present in leaves. Cooler temperatures and other environmental factors can also influence the red and purple colors associated with anthocyanin pigments.

Because Maine's forests contain such a diverse mix of tree species and growing conditions, the result is a constantly changing mosaic of color throughout the season.

New: Share Your Fall Event with Maine Foliage Visitors

For 2026, DACF is inviting organizations, communities, farms, nonprofits, municipalities, and event organizers to submit public fall events for possible inclusion in Maine's Weekly Foliage Reports. DACF is looking for more activities that give residents and visitors another reason to get out and experience autumn in Maine, including:

  • Harvest festivals and agricultural fairs
  • Farm and food events
  • Outdoor recreation and nature-based activities
  • Arts and cultural events
  • Community festivals and celebrations
  • Other public events that complement the fall foliage experience

Events should take place during Maine's fall foliage reporting season, generally mid-September through mid-October, and must be open to the public.

SUBMIT YOUR FALL EVENT

DACF will review events based on timing, location, relevance to the foliage season, and available space. Submitted information may be edited for length, clarity, and style.

Follow the Color at MaineFoliage.com

Throughout the season, MaineFoliage.com is the official resource for tracking Maine's changing fall color. Weekly reports provide foliage conditions across the state and help residents and visitors decide when and where to explore. The first report will be published on Wednesday, September 9, 2026, with updated reports following every Wednesday through the foliage season.

From Maine's northern forests and western mountains to its lakes, farms, downtowns, and coast, there is no single way to experience fall in Maine. Following the changing color and exploring the places, people, events, and landscapes along the way is part of what makes the season special.

About Maine's Fall Foliage Reports

For 68 years, the DACF has produced Maine's official fall foliage reports, drawing on observations from forestry and conservation professionals across the state. Published weekly throughout the season, the reports track the progression of color and leaf drop across seven foliage zones and provide information and resources to help residents and visitors make the most of Maine's spectacular fall season.

entry.title: Maine DEP Initiates Legal Action Against Mallinckrodt US LLC to Address Cleanup Failures at Orrington Site
entry.content:
Maine DEP Initiates Legal Action Against Mallinckrodt US LLC to Address Cleanup Failures at Orrington Site

Maine Department of Environmental Protection sent this bulletin at 08/25/2026 03:45 PM EDT

--- PRESS RELEASE ---

For Immediate Release

 

Maine DEP Initiates Legal Action Against Mallinckrodt US LLC to Address Cleanup Failures at Orrington Site

 

AUGUSTA, August 25, 2026 — The Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) filed a formal complaint today in Penobscot County Superior Court against Mallinckrodt US LLC (Mallinckrodt). The complaint details the failure by Mallinckrodt to complete cleanup of the former Holtrachem site located along the Penobscot River in Orrington, Maine, one of Maine’s most contaminated sites. Mallinckrodt has not met the remediation standards required in the DEP’s 2008 Designation of Uncontrolled Hazardous Substance Site and Order, that was affirmed in 2010 by the Board of Environmental Protection (BEP) in its own slightly modified order, affirmed in 2012 by the Maine Business and Consumer Docket, and finally affirmed in 2014 by the Maine Supreme Judicial Court sitting as the Law Court.

The former Holtrachem site was a chloralkali manufacturing facility, which made chemicals commonly used in the pulp and paper industry. Historic operations resulted in a significant amount of contamination, including highly toxic mercury and chloropicrin, in surrounding soils, groundwaters, and the Penobscot River. Site-specific standards were established by the DEP and BEP Orders to ensure that the site would be cleaned up in a manner that would protect public health, safety, and the environment.  Despite these Orders, large areas of soils still remain on site that exceed the site-specific cleanup standards.

The DEP has worked diligently to provide oversight during cleanup of the former Holtrachem site to ensure that Mallinckrodt conducts remediation in compliance with the DEP and BEP Orders. While progress has been made, it began to slow down as early as 2018 when Mallinckrodt began the first of several attempts to seek relief from meeting the Orders’ requirements. Since 2023, Mallinckrodt has ceased any meaningful progress toward remediation at the site.

Prior to today’s filing, two Notices of Violation (NOVs) were issued to Mallinckrodt on March 19, 2025, and October 22, 2025. These NOVs provide more detailed information about Mallinckrodt’s failure to comply with the DEP and BEP Orders. Copies of these NOVs are available on the DEP Mallinckrodt webpage.

The Department is seeking injunctive relief from the Penobscot Superior Court and civil penalties for ongoing violations.
